# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. The Rover (2014): Has anyone seen this film?

**Score:** 44
**Body:** I just rewatched this film with my girlfriend the other night. It is a masterpiece of minimalism. It's bleak, poignant, atmospheric, and has a career-best performance from Guy Pearce (the best actor working today, imo). The themes center around despair and finding hope in a bleak world, hatred and love (and the underlying connection between them), and keeping your humanity in the face of extreme hardship. 

Has anyone else seen this? I'd love to discuss what anyone else thought of the film's central questions and themes, as well as the filmmaking more broadly. 

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Not since around the time it came out, but yea really good movie, sorta like an updated more realistic version of the first Mad Max. Between this and Animal Kingdom I thought Michod was gonna be a big thing, I do know people like The King but never got around to it, and obviously Christy was a fiasco.
  - The Mad Max analogy is a good one; I thought the same thing. As for Michod, I think he started breaking into Hollywood and stopped doing Australian films, and I think that hasn't worked as well for him.  He clearly works better on indie films than Hollywood studio movies. I'd be stoked if he announced another Australian film and reunited with Guy Pearce and Ben Mendelsohn. 

The King was one of the most plain, mediocre films I have ever seen. It's not even bad; everything about it is just so "meh". It's one of the only films I have ever seen where I felt nothing about it whatsoever by the end. 
    - I really like The King. It feels so real, and Joel Edgerton is just one of the coolest actors in Hollywood. I saw it on a projector though, I think it hits differently on a bigger screen. It's also one of the only films where I actually see Chalamet as a character lol. I can see how the narration is rather simple and heavy-handed, but atmosphere and direction in particular are great.
2. When I watched this in the cinema I thought someone’s phone was playing Pretty Girl Rock by Keri Hilson in the middle of film - because it seemed to be such a departure from the narrative - and then eventually Robert Pattinson starts singing to the track in the vehicle at night.
3. It’s sort of a the other side of the coin from a thematically similar film like The Road (another Aussie director coincidentally). The knots we twist ourselves into when pressed to adapt to extreme situations and how those knots can calcify over time. When you need to connect with your humanity again, it’s not always easy. Those are the sorts of ideas it brings up for me.

I saw an early screening in Austin with Guy Pearce (agree he’s amazing) there for a Q&A and although I honestly remember nothing of the Q&A, I really loved the film. It was the first non-Twilight thing I ever saw Robert Pattinson in and it really made me notice his chops. David Michôd’s Animal Kingdom from 2010 was stellar and even War Machine is worth seeing IMO. I’ve been meaning to watch The King.
4. I really like this movie. [The trailer still gives me a few chills.](
https://youtu.be/ChM2icbWo9w?si=Iw3qt02n9SXHTVEm)

I’ve been a fan of Guy Pearce since his breakout in LA Confidential. I still say the biggest crime Prometheus committed was making his Weyland character an old man under a ton of aging makeup instead of the fiery version we got in the [TED Talk teaser.](
https://youtu.be/E4SSU29Arj0?si=Vayc0uOnBKMkyKX9).

For Robert Pattinson, this was his first film after Twilight was behind him, and it was a great opportunity to display his talents.

Definitely a great film on what the world would be like after a major catastrophe or societal collapse. Guy Pearce talking about the horrible thing he did and yet nobody showing up to punish him is a scene that still sticks with me.
5. I'm so pleased to see someone give this film some recognition here.  I discovered it about three years ago and have rewatched it at least three additional times.  I was impressed by how the director, David Michod, keeps a quiet steady tone throughout the film, puncturing the bleakness only with short bursts of violence.  There's a grittiness here rarely found in Hollywood movies these days (the characters actually sweat, but we're in Australia after all).

Agreed, Mr. Pearce is always worth watching, even in the **Mildred Pierce** miniseries (HBO/2011) directed by Todd Haynes.
6. Great flick. I rewatch it every now and again as it's a masterclass in brood and mood. Pearce's posture and gait are something to behold and it was also the film where I realized hey that Pattinson guy can actually act
7.  The Rover is brilliant. One of the best films of this century. I agree completely with people who feel it's the true inheritor of the legacy of the original Mad Max film, the other sequels went very far afield from the realistic original. 

 I was actually thinking about this one recently, was reminded of how many people hated the Pattinson hire as Batman because he was the teen vampire guy which made me realize how underground The Rover was. It was a similar experience to hearing people hate on the Daniel Craig hire as James Bond and subsequent realization that not very many had seen Layer Cake.
8. Yes excellent movie. Very dark. Guy Pearce plays a likeable psychopath. Lol.  If I remember the movie properly he is evil because he wants to see what he can get away ? Sort of like the Comedian in Watchmen. 
  Was there a scene where he suddenly shoots a dwarf for mistreatment of a dog? 
  I loved the (a)morality of the movie

## 2. Harakiri (1962)

**Score:** 38
**Body:** When I saw this film was rated as the greatest film ever made on letterboxd, I honestly didn't expect much. I expected it to be pretentious, boring, and preachy.

Holy shit. I think everyone's right. This might be the all-time greatest film ever made. It should be studied as one of the seminal texts of cinema. It feels like a Kurosawa film, but with a different coating of style that mainly comes from a subtlety that his films often lack. It was culturally relevant to the time, however it's universally relevant to us all now. I'm truly shocked at how much I loved this film, specifically how it raises ideas about the traditions that we set, and how easily people are willing to exploit them.

It actually reminded me of The Odyssey in some ways (though I think it's safe to say this film is significantly better). Both films take place in ancient times, use a non-linear structure that often tells side-stories through the character's recollecting past events, but most importantly, both films use these features to critique the traditions set for them. In The Odyssey, Nolan critiques the idea of Zeus' Law, displaying the people who are willing to exploit it for power. Harakiri does a similar thing with the idea of honor. I would be fascinated to know if anyone else picked up on this, or whether Nolan ever said anything about taking inspiration from Harakiri.

If you've been putting this one off, you really should watch it. It's one of the greatest films I've ever seen.

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The screenwriter Shinobu Hashimoto also wrote Seven Samurai and several other Kurosawa films (Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, I Live in Fear, The Bad Sleep Well) so no surprise it feels like a Kurosawa film. 

And if you like Kobayashi's Harakiri, check out his epic WWII movie The Human Condition. It might be even better.
  - Human Condition series might just be my favorite trilogy of all time. Each movie in the trilogy is better than the last. Like, Kaji's tribulations were horrifying to watch and I felt seriously bad for him throughout. I also am very fond of Kobayashi's portrayal of Japanese army, his frustrations with their conduct during the war, his refusal to serve as well as his subsequent imprisonment. You can feel Kobayashi's rational vitriol throughout. These films were absolutely heartbreaking to sit through, but was absolutely worth it. 
2. It's one of my favorite movies. I watched it without knowing anything about it because I liked samurai stuff and a movie about a seppuku was intriguing. It's completely insane how it wraps you slowly turning your mind from considering these beggar samurai faking a death wish for money, into just straight up hating the entire system and wanting to burn it all down. It's incredible.


3. You have to remember that the top films on letterboxd are there because thousands and thousands of people think the film is incredible. Most of the stuff in the top fifty or so is pretty accessible. It's more of a popularity gauge than anything else.

Harakiri is a prime example. It's so strong in every category that it's hard to imagine most movie nerds on letterboxd wouldn't like it.

Also I'd definitely try to shed the 'high rated equals boring/pretentious' connection. I've definitely seen movies that have soured me on greats/classics (like citizen kane which i can appreciate but don't care to ever sit through again) but most of them are classic for a reason and hold up amazingly well today, especially when most of the classics are marked by expert lighting, practical effects and wonderful sets/locations and many modern films have none of those things.
  - Yeah "didn't expect much from the highest rated movie" is so weird 
4. Kobayashi was one of a handful of filmmakers who put into a very neat dialectic traditional Japanese aesthetics which he loved and the multitudes of problems with Japanese society and customs (Kurosawa, Mizoguchi, Okamoto and Shinoda all did this quite well), but Kobayashi stands out for his ruthlessly clear eyed vision and very precise and carefully choreographed action sequences with static compositions that tell the entire story in themselves, he was a master who unfortunately was hit hard by the collapse of the studio system in Japan and ostracized by a lot of the public owing to his willingness to speak up about the inhumanity of Japanese conservatism, he didn't just critique the militarism that swept up Japan into fascism but about Japanese society in general, he always stood up very bravely to the ways Japanese customs and traditions dehumanize many, I think he does it best in Harakiri.  
.  
 It is interesting to note that despite his mastery of the jidaigeki (Harakiri easily being among the best of them) it is not really a genre he worked in a lot, he he only made 4 period pieces and his favorite films and passion projects went in other directions, one of his most personal projects that was unfortunately never made was a movie about the ancient Chinese ruins among the silk road, I think he lived with regret that it was never made his entire life (it was actually written and planned well before Harakiri and the last part of the Human Condition). I'd recommend some of his later works such as Hymn to a Tired Man AKA Youth of Japan, Kaseki, and Inn of Evil, his last period film. All are superb works that are just as good as Harakiri imo, I think Kobayashi's reputation should extend well beyond his early 60s period masterpieces.
5. Great film. I think Samurai Rebellion may be even better but it has been 15 years since I watched either of them. Very intense, masterful compositions. 

Never enjoyed The Human Condition, unfortunately. 

## 3. Does it actually make sense to characterize the ending of Schindler's List as "comforting" and "happy"? I enjoy and respect Gilliam's work as much as the next person, but watching this interview clip from him made me feel like we watched two COMPLETELY different movies!

**Score:** 11
**Body:** [https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=CAKS3rdYTpI&pp=ygUedGVycnkgZ2lsbGlhbSBzY2hpbmRsZXIncyBsaXN0&ra=m](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=CAKS3rdYTpI&pp=ygUedGVycnkgZ2lsbGlhbSBzY2hpbmRsZXIncyBsaXN0&ra=m)

**(After thinking about it more, I have extensively edited this post since I first made it and I apologize if that has made any of the older replies here confusing to anybody. This was not long enough to post as a reply itself and got deleted, so that is why I‘m putting it up here)**

Is it also too simplistic/derisive to characterize Schindler's List as a whole as just being a film about “success” without showing the true horrors of the Holocaust, rather than being about the constant struggle to survive in brutal conditions, being able to have some hope even in the darkest times of the world’s history, humanity *still* being able to break through in horrific situations, the massive differences that even *one* person can make in hundreds of people’s lives even when powerful sadistic forces/people are against them, or any other much deeper, richer messages that (I also believe) can be found in this movie?

Furthermore, do movies being comforting or having happy endings in general *really* mean that they’re inherently dumber or worse than more ambiguous/cynical ones? Is this true for films that give audiences definitive answers and conclusions to/in their stories as well? I don't believe this myself, because I think that happy endings, comforting stories, and definitive answers/conclusions are all things that CAN be written incredibly thoughtfully and skillfully in movies, as Steven Spielberg himself has routinely demonstrated. I also really don’t believe that those are inherently negative things for movies to be in general! Making movies comforting or satisfying for an audience to watch *can* be inherently *good* things for them to be, as long as the story is written with them in mind and it makes sense for the plot/characters. I additionally think that movies can also provide good/satisfying answers to audiences about the characters, themes, events, etc. in their stories and still leave people personally thinking critically or having thoughtful discussions with other folks about them.

I also think that making a movie about the Holocaust telling the story about the survival of over 1,000 Jewish people *from* that civilizational failure. *FROM* that genocide and the other horrors/evils that took place during it was/is an *extremely* important and valuable story to tell, especially from one of the most famous Jewish directors of all time.

Now, to reiterate, this is in *no* way meant to trivialize/discredit Terry Gilliam's own talent or the wonderfully creative movies that he himself has made, of course! However, that being said, I also do believe that this is an (to say the least!) *extremely* bad-faith perspective/reading to have on Spielberg and his work in general from Gilliam, and I think that he harshly insults both without ever providing good enough reasons TO be so harsh/nasty about them in this interview in the first place. Quite frankly, I also consider such a bitter, deeply combative critique to be fairly out of character for Gilliam as a person, although I don't believe that I've watched enough interviews from him to say that definitively.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Obviously, this is in the context of being a Holocaust movie, the vast majority of which involve terribly tragic endings.

The first time I saw the film, I remember getting to the end and thinking, “of course, this is how Spielberg does a Holocaust film—by focusing on a story of people who were saved.”

It is comforting and “optimistic” within the context of being a film about the Holocaust (note: not just a WWII movie, but one directly about the extermination of the Jews). His comments are a bit hyperbolic, but I get what he’s saying.
  - This is it. It's an amazing story to be sure, and well worth to be told. But he has a point.

Claude Lanzmann, the director of Shoah, the arguably most renowned documentary about the Holocaust out there, and one of the most renowned documentaries of all time at that, criticized Schindler's List for that too. He found to depict the Holocaust in a conventional theatrical movie narrative inherently problematic.

He basically argued that the Holocaust wasn't a story with classic beginning, heroes and resolution. But the film gives you catharsis and hope, when for most Jews it was just horror and death. Shoah's approach is the exact opposite: no staged scenes, no heroes, no redemption, only people remembering, and... many people not wanting to remember. In my opinion both approaches are extremely valuable if done right.

But I will say, [Shoah](https://youtu.be/S7z8lOvfskk?si=KYSjaIS_V505EEmT) hits differently.

3. I haven’t watched the Gilliam clip, but I have read your post. I absolutely share the view that big budget commercial period films like Schindler’s List are designed to be comforting. Hollywood’s obsession with heroes and heroism turns complex and disturbing periods of history into comforting fairytales with goodies and baddies. It’s reductive and exploitative, and it’s what Hollywood has been doing to history since the height of the Western genre. You can find it in all sorts of other historically set films: Green Book is another good example.

Three far more honest and sensitive films about the Holocaust which come to mind are The Zone of Interest, Son of Saul and A Real Pain and I would strongly recommend those - they demonstrate how an atrocity can be turned into a story without being reductive or exploitative.

I suppose there's no way to quantify these sorts of things, but I would say that more or less every scene in the film is always about both those two things: the relationship (Benji is a 'real pain') and the theme I identified (what is 'real pain'?).

The theme was not "window dressing" in any way: it had a lot to say about it. Both characters went on a symbolic journey to investigate what the connection they felt to the holocaust through their heritage meant to them, and every scene explored how it affected both men differently.

I didn't get the sense that he thought movies should be strictly one type or the other, just that he personally finds Kubrick more satisfying and interesting. I don't find Gilliam particularly bitter here, but he has a reputation for bluntness and a sharply critical tongue. I just see a guy with a high profile giving his opinion. He simplified what Schindler's List is about but I don't think he's wrong. 5. This is an old argument, and better filmmakers than Gilliam have made it. Michael Haneke infamously hated it. Stanley Kubrick said something to the effect of “the holocaust is about 8 million Jews who died, Schindlers List is about 800 who didn’t.” I agree with you that it’s fundamentally kind of lame to look at art that way, as if there’s only one way you’re allowed to make a movie about the holocaust, and I think it’s wrong to act like choosing to make a movie about people who were saved somehow invalidates the stories of the many people who weren’t.

Is there room for nuance here, of course there is. Did Spielberg err in making his Nazi too evil to be believable? Is the gas chamber scene emotionally manipulative? These are questions that are worth asking and worth hearing our opposing views from. But a lot of the arguments seem to boil down to “Spielberg erred by making his movie about Oskar Schindler in the first place, he should have made a movie with a Jewish protagonist or a movie that ends in death”, and I don’t really buy that.
6. For Jews throughout history,  telling tales of survival in the face of antisemitism and in this case genocide have incredible power and a prominent place among the generational legacy of a people. 

To say that only tales of defeat are acceptable denies those who overcame the horrors of Shoah the ability to tell their stories. It silences those whose lived experience can be an inspiration to later generations when antisemitism again rears its ugly, persistent head.

I will take an "uplifting" story about real people who survived (or didn't) 100% of the time over fictional accounts that had to be fabricated because the real people didn't survive to tell their own story.
